2.36

G. Asking questions

In German, as in English, there are three kinds of questions:


"Wer-wie-was" questions

Wer ist das?

Wie findest du den Campus?

Was machst du heute Abend?

Who ist that?

What do you think of the campus?

What are you doing this evening?

Verb-first questions

Bist du auf Twitter?

Heißt du Lukas?

Are you on Twitter?

Is your name Lukas?

Tag questions

Spotify ist cool, oder?

Das ist Deutsch, nicht wahr?

Spotify is cool, isn’t it?

That's German, right?

G.1

"Wer-wie-was" questions

These questions begin with a question word, most of which you've already encountered:

wer … ?

wann … ?

wie … ?

wie viel … ?

wie viele … ?

wieso … ?

wo … ?

warum … ?

woher … ?

was … ?

was für … ?

who … ?

when … ?

how … ?

how much … ?

how many … ?

how come / why … ?

where … ?

why … ?

from where … ? (i.e., origin)

what … ?

what kind of … ?

A few examples:

Wie viele Kurse machst du?

How many courses are you taking?

Wann arbeitest du ?

When do you work?

When are you working?

Warum arbeitest du so viel?

Why do you work so much?

Why are you working so much?

Sometimes these are referred to as “open” or “general” questions, since there is no pre-determined answer such as yes or no. As you can see in the examples above, English “Wh-questions” are similar to these, but differ in that English often requires an auxiliary verb after the question word (do ... work / are ... working) as well as changes to the main verb (work vs. working). German only requires one verb, which always conjugates with the sentence subject. (And you thought German was more complicated than English.)

G.2.

Verb-first questions

These questions begin with a conjugated verb, followed by the sentence subject. They are sometimes called “yes/no” or “closed” questions, since a narrow range of answers is expected, such as yes, no or maybe.

Haben deine Eltern viele Facebook-Freunde?

Do your parents have a lot of Facebook friends?

Spielt er noch Super Mario?

Is he still playing ... / Does he still play Super Mario?

Wohnen sie auf dem Campus?

Are they living ... / Do they live on campus?

Schreibt sie einen Blog?

Is she writing ... / Does she write a blog?

Here too, German is simpler than English, with only one option for the conjugated verb.

content:
G.3

Tag questions

A tag question is a statement that has been turned into a question by means of an added phrase:

You understand that, right?

He’s on Instagram again, isn’t he?

We need some more time, don’t we?

It’s nice today, isn’t it?


These are tricky in English. With the exception of right?, an English question tag must reflect the subject, verb tense, and positive/negative sense of the preceiding statement:

You understand that, don’t you?

She knew that, didn't she?

That's not easy, is it?

He plays well, doesn’t he?

We don’t have much time, do we?

It’s nice today, isn’t it?

Once again, German is simpler here than English. Its two question tags — nicht wahr and oder — remain fixed no matter what's in the statement, and can be used interchangeably. (NB: In this usage, wahr and oder no longer carry their respective literal meanings of true and or.)

Using these to translate the English questions above:

Du verstehst das, oder? / Du verstehst das, nicht wahr?

Sie wusste das, nicht wahr? / Sie wusste das, oder?

Das ist nicht einfach, nicht wahr? / Das ist nicht einfach, oder?

Er spielt gut, oder? / Er spielt gut, nicht wahr?

Wir haben nicht viel Zeit, oder? / Wir haben nicht viel Zeit, nicht wahr?

Es ist schön heute, nicht wahr? / Es ist schön heute, oder?

H. Possessive adjectives: mein / dein / …


H.1

As soon as you learn how to say family or friends, you naturally want to refer to my family or your friends. German, like English, lets you do this with a set of possessive adjectives that correspond to each of the personal pronouns you’ve learned.


singular plural
first-person ich → mein wir → unser
second-person du → dein

Sie → Ihr

 ihr → euer

Sie → Ihr
third-person

er/der Mann → sein

sie/die Frau → ihr

es/das Kind → sein

 sie/die Leute → ihr

Notice that German (unlike French or Spanish) distinguishes between his and her, using sein and ihr. Notice too that there are several overlapping forms: his and its are both expressed with sein; and her, their and your (formal) all translate with ihr / Ihr.

H.1
label: H.1

content:
H.2

Using possessive adjectives to modify nouns requires keeping track of the case and gender of the noun. To see how this works in practice, listen to the following noun phrases, and click on the form that precedes each noun. (All of the nouns here are taken from the core vocabulary list for this chapter.

1. (mein meine) Kind
2. (mein meine) Antwort
3. (mein meine) Computer
4. (mein meine) Mutter
5. (mein meine) Vater
6. (mein meine) Eltern
7. (mein meine) Familie
8. (mein meine) Beispiel
9. (mein meine) Beziehung
10. (mein meine) Bruder

Notice the strong correlation between this usage and the way German distinguishes between ein and eine, depending on the gender of the noun following it:

masculine feminine neuter

ein Mann

ein Bruder

ein Abend

ein Computer

eine Frau

eine Antwort

eine Aufgabe

eine Beziehung

ein Kind

ein Beispiel

ein Land

ein Netz

Possessive adjectives follow the same pattern, ending in -e when they precede feminine (and plural) nouns, and taking no ending with masculine and neuter singular nouns. This is why possessive adjectives are often called ein-words.

masculine feminine neuter
ein Sohn eine Tochter ein Kind
mein Bruder meine Antwort mein Beispiel
dein Abend deine Aufgabe dein Land
sein Computer seine Beziehung sein Internet

A few additional points:

  • When euer takes an ending, it normally drops the -e- in the middle of the word: euer + -e → eure.)

  • Remember: When possessive adjectives modify plural nouns (in the nominative case), they take an -e ending regardless of gender, just like keine:

    meine Brüder

    deine Aufgaben

    ihre Kinder

  • German possessive adjectives specify the gender of who (or what) is doing the possessing — sein Bruder vs. ihr Bruder. Their endings, in turn, reflect the gender of the noun following the adjective: sein Bruder vs. seine Schwester, ihr Bruder vs. ihre Schwester.
